design_detail: Systematic review with a thematic (narrative) synthesis and no meta-analysis of studies published from January 2000 to November 2011, in English or Dutch, on health professionals' attitudes towards patients with alcohol or illicit drug use disorders in Western countries, the explanations offered for negative attitudes, and the consequences of those attitudes for healthcare delivery. PubMed, PsycINFO and Embase were searched; 1562 records remained after duplicates were removed and 28 papers were included (Australia 12, UK 7, USA 5, Canada 1, Ireland 1, one eight-country European comparison and one USA–UK comparison), five of which come from two shared samples. The included studies are mostly cross-sectional questionnaire surveys of professionals' self-reported attitudes, with interview and focus-group studies, two implicit association tests and two studies using observation; the review describes no randomized experiment, and the one vignette study (Rao et al., 2009) compared described patient types. Study quality was rated with 11 indicators taken from Buckley et al. (2009); all 28 met at least 7 and were weighted equally. No protocol or registration is mentioned.
can_establish: What 28 papers from 2000–2011 in Australia, the UK, Ireland, North America and eight European countries reported about health professionals' self-reported attitudes towards patients with alcohol or drug use disorders, the explanations those studies offered, and how few of them examined consequences for care.
cannot_establish: How common negative attitudes are (there are no counts or pooled estimates, and several included studies found moderate, neutral or positive attitudes); that negative attitudes cause poorer care or outcomes (the consequence evidence is a handful of qualitative, mixed-methods and cross-sectional studies, one with a null result and one, not discussed, finding better care); whether training improves attitudes (studies of education and training were excluded, and the associations cited are cross-sectional); or anything about Asia, Africa, South America or studies after 2011.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable at review level. PubMed, PsycINFO and Embase were searched for articles published from January 2000 to November 2011 in English or Dutch; the PubMed strategy is printed, with very similar versions said to have been used for the other two databases. The strategy combined health-personnel, substance-use-disorder and attitude terms with care-delivery or stigma terms (sets #30 to #33). No grey literature, reference-list, citation or expert searching is described (2.1, p. 24; Table 1, p. 26; Fig. 1, p. 25).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: studies of the attitudes of health professionals (or of professionals together with students) towards patients with alcohol or illicit drug use disorders, and studies of stigma, perception or healthcare delivery as a consequence of these attitudes; reviews, commentaries and letters were excluded. Excluded: attitudes towards specific subgroups (pregnant women, sexual or ethnic minorities, because of double stigma), towards screening and identification, or towards treatments (methadone maintenance, needle and syringe provision, 12-step programs); studies of medical students only; studies from Asia, Africa and South America, excluded at the full-text stage as culturally, historically and socially different; studies of a very specific setting or explicit subgroup (Table 2, p. 26; 2.2, pp. 24–25). Records concerning education, training or students were excluded at screening (34 abstracts and 4 full texts; Fig. 1, p. 25).
sample.demographics: Professional groups (3.2, p. 26): seven papers studied a mix of professions, eight nurses, seven staff of addiction or mental health services, four physicians and one physicians and nurses; five also included patients. Sample sizes in Table 4 range from 8 interviewed professionals (Brener et al., 2010b) to 1,605 nurses (Ford et al., 2008, 2009); Ding et al. (2005) also surveyed 2,864 patients with HIV, and Segal & Dittrich (2001) observed 683 psychiatric emergency visits from 1985–1986 (Table 4, pp. 27–29). Years of data collection are not otherwise given.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Response rates in Table 4, where given, range from 31% (May et al., 2002) to 92% (Saitz et al., 2002); all workshop attendees took part in Strauser et al. (2009); several papers give none (pp. 27–29).
sample.selection_effects: Three databases, of which PsycINFO contributed only 10 records against 1170 from PubMed and 395 from Embase, without comment; a search requiring care-delivery or stigma terms alongside attitude terms; English and Dutch only; 31 records excluded because no abstract or full text was available; 10 full texts excluded because the studies came from Asia, Africa or South America; and exclusion of studies of training, screening and attitudes to treatments. The primary studies drew self-selected respondents, with response rates as low as 31%; the authors note that only motivated professionals take part in such studies (4.1, p. 33).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable at review level. The target of the attitudes is the patient group each study asked about, in that study's own terms (2.3, p. 25): people who inject drugs (some with hepatitis C or HIV), people who use illicit drugs or opiates, people with alcohol problems, people with a dual diagnosis, cocaine addiction among other conditions, and patients with substance use problems in general (Tables 4 and 5, pp. 27–32).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable. Attitudes towards patients with alcohol and with illicit drug problems are combined in the synthesis; the only contrast by substance reported in the text is that regard was especially low for patients who use drugs (Gilchrist et al., 2011; 3.3, p. 26).

comparison.controls: None at review level: comparison was declared not applicable (2.1, p. 24). Within primary studies, attitudes were compared with those towards other patient groups (depression and diabetes, Gilchrist et al., 2011; schizophrenia and forensic patients, Rao et al., 2009; depression and hypertension, Saitz et al., 2002; AIDS, psychosis, depression, cancer and intellectual disability (printed as 'mental retardation'), Strauser et al., 2009; other psychiatric emergency patients, Segal & Dittrich, 2001), between professions or settings, and by contact, experience or training (Tables 4 and 5).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level. The professional characteristics offered as explanations (contact, experience, training, role support) were measured at the same time as attitudes in the primary studies, so their direction of influence is not established.

outcomes.instruments: The primary studies used the Substance Abuse Attitude Survey (called a Scale in the text; 5 papers), the Alcohol and Alcohol Problems Perception Questionnaire or its drug version (4 papers by the text; Table 5 names the alcohol version for Ford et al., 2008 and 2009, one sample, and the drug version for Albery et al., 2003 and Howard & Holmshaw, 2010), the Medical Condition Regard Scale, the Attitude to Mental Illness Questionnaire with vignettes, the Addiction Beliefs Scale, the Psychiatric Disability Attribution Questionnaire, implicit association tests, quality-of-care indices applied to observed visits, and interviews or focus groups (3.2, p. 26; Table 5, pp. 30–32).
outcomes.validity_norms: Study quality was judged with 11 indicators from Buckley et al. (2009), a review of portfolios in undergraduate medical education: research question, subjects, data collection, completeness of data (attrition under 50%, acceptable response rate), control for confounding, analysis, conclusions, reproducibility, prospective design, ethics and triangulation; a study was of acceptable quality if it met at least 7 (Table 3, p. 26). All 28 passed and were weighted equally; ratings by study are not reported (3.1, 1st paragraph, continued on p. 26).
outcomes.operationalization: The review does not define a negative attitude; it keeps each study's terms and measures (2.3, p. 25). Consequences for healthcare delivery covered patients' perceived discrimination and treatment completion, patients' views of their professionals, patient-reported problems with care, and professionals' accounts of their own practice; one included study measured quality of care from observed visits (Segal & Dittrich, 2001).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Titles were screened by one reviewer, with a random 10% screened by a second (94% agreement); abstracts and full texts were assessed by two independent reviewers, with disagreements settled by discussion or a third reviewer; data were extracted by one reviewer and verified by a second (2.2 and 2.3, pp. 24–25).

analysis.effect_sizes: None. A thematic synthesis without pooled estimates, effect sizes or counts of studies by direction of finding (2.3, p. 25). The only figures carried from primary studies are descriptive, for example that 23.2% of the patients in Ding et al. (2005), described in Table 5 as HIV and IDU patients, had physicians with negative attitudes towards patients who inject drugs (Table 5, p. 30).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the PRISMA explanation paper (Liberati et al., 2009) is cited only for the PICO approach used to build search terms (2.1, p. 24).
analysis.selective_reporting: The one included study that measured quality of care from observed visits (Segal & Dittrich, 2001: better care for patients with substance use problems than for other psychiatric emergency patients on all four criteria) appears only in Tables 4 and 5 and is not mentioned in the text, including the section on consequences (3.5, pp. 32–33). Studies with positive findings are mentioned as a contrast (3.3, p. 29) without a count of studies in each direction.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 28 papers (at most 25 independent samples), many studies, mostly cross-sectional self-report surveys and qualitative studies from Australia, the UK and the USA, reported negative attitudes, or lower regard for patients with substance use disorders than for other patients, especially among professionals outside addiction services; at least six papers' summaries in Table 5 describe moderate, neutral, appropriate or positive attitudes. More contact, experience, training and role support went with more positive attitudes in cross-sectional data. On consequences, one mixed-methods study found that clients' perceived staff discrimination predicted dropping out of treatment, one cross-sectional study linked professionals' attitudes to patients' views of them, two qualitative studies described disempowerment and shorter, task-oriented visits, one large survey found no association between physicians' attitudes and patients' reports of their care, and one observational study found better care for patients with substance use problems.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states as findings that negative attitudes "diminished patients' feelings of empowerment and subsequent treatment outcomes" and that a more task-oriented approach results in less personal engagement and diminished empathy, and concludes that negative attitudes are common and "contribute to suboptimal health care" (abstract, p. 23). In the Results these statements rest on one qualitative study of treatment staff and consumers (Curtis & Harrison, 2001) and one qualitative study of 18 district nurses (Peckover & Chidlaw, 2007), and are worded with 'may' (3.5, p. 33); the treatment-completion finding is attributed to the wrong Brener paper (p. 32); the null finding of Ding et al. (2005) is mentioned but not weighed; and the observational study finding better care (Segal & Dittrich, 2001) is not mentioned. That professionals generally had negative attitudes is a narrative judgment without a count. The recommendation of more education and training (4.2, p. 33) rests on cross-sectional associations, after records concerning education or training were excluded at screening (Fig. 1, p. 25). The abstract does end by noting that few studies have evaluated consequences.

timeline.event: Howard and Chung, review of nurses' attitudes towards patients who misuse substances, cited in the Introduction as finding greater acceptance although a minority regarded these patients as immoral and unlikely to recover (p. 24); not read.
This review: 28 papers published 2000–2011 on health professionals' attitudes towards patients with alcohol or drug use disorders; few examined consequences for care.
Bielenberg et al., systematic review of stigma interventions for providers who treat patients with substance use disorders (on the project's language-and-stigma list; not read).
Pavone et al., systematic review of interventions to reduce clinician stigma toward people with opioid use disorder (on the project's language-and-stigma list; not read).

replication.where_it_stands: The project's language-and-stigma list named this review as its largest gap. It summarizes the literature to 2011 only, from Western countries, and does not quantify how common negative attitudes are; the evidence it gathered on consequences for care was thin and pointed in different directions. The later reviews on the project's lists concern interventions to reduce clinician stigma; none has been appraised for this card, so whether the question of consequences has since been answered is not known from the sources read.

funding.affiliations_note: Tranzo, Tilburg School of Social and Behavioral Sciences, Tilburg University (all four authors); Phrenos Centre of Expertise, Utrecht, and Parnassia Bavo Group, Dijk en Duin Mental Health Center, Castricum (van Weeghel) (p. 23). None of the authors is an author of an included study (editors' check of the reference list, pp. 34–35).

what_would_settle_it: A registered, updated systematic review with appraisal reported study by study, a list of excluded studies and no regional exclusion, which counts and where possible pools attitude findings by profession and patient group; and prospective studies linking clinicians' measured attitudes to the care actually delivered (observed or from records) and to patients' retention and outcomes, adjusting for the patients' severity.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (health personnel), exposure (patients with alcohol or illicit drug use disorders as the target of attitudes) and outcomes (attitudes, healthcare delivery, stigma) are set out with the PICO approach, but the comparison is declared not applicable (2.1, p. 24); judged no, as for other reviews without a comparator in this project.
No protocol or registration is mentioned.

All original studies were eligible, quantitative and qualitative, and reviews, commentaries and letters were excluded (abstract; Fig. 1); a brief reason for including both quantitative and qualitative studies is given, but only in the Discussion (4.1, p. 33).

Three databases, the PubMed strategy printed (Table 1) and a date range justified by the aim of recent evidence; but English and Dutch only without justification (named only as a limitation, 4.1), no grey literature, reference lists, citation searching or experts, records without an abstract or full text excluded (31), and only 10 records from PsycINFO, unexplained. Judged no on the project's reading of item 4 (decision p-amstar2-item4).
Abstracts and full texts assessed by two independent reviewers; titles by one reviewer with a random 10% double-screened (94% agreement) (2.2, pp. 24–25).

Extraction by one reviewer, verified by a second, with disparities resolved by discussion and rereading the original studies (2.3, p. 25); judged yes as for other reviews in this project in which a second reviewer checked the extraction.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Fig. 1 gives counts by reason only; the 27 excluded full texts are not listed.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 4 gives country, population, sample size, setting and design, and Table 5 instruments and main results; the patient group targeted, years of data collection, several response rates and the direction of each finding are not given systematically.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: An 11-item checklist from a review of educational portfolios (Buckley et al., 2009), with items on confounding, appropriateness of subjects, validity of data collection and completeness or response rate, was applied by two reviewers at full text (Table 3; Fig. 1); but every study passed a 7-of-11 threshold, the same checklist was applied to qualitative studies, and no ratings are reported study by study.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: No meta-analysis; thematic synthesis because of heterogeneous populations, designs and settings (2.3, p. 25).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: All studies were weighted equally because all passed the quality threshold (3.1, 1st paragraph, continued on p. 26). The limitations mention self-selection of motivated respondents and social desirability in the primary studies (4.1, p. 33), but the abstract's causal statements about consequences and the recommendation of training are drawn from qualitative and cross-sectional studies without discussing those designs' limits.

Variation in attitudes is related narratively to discipline, contact, experience, training and support (3.3 and 3.4), but studies with positive or neutral findings are listed without explaining why they differ, the null result of Ding et al. (2005) on care is noted without discussion, and the observational study finding better care (Segal & Dittrich, 2001) is not mentioned.
No quantitative synthesis; publication bias is not discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding ('Nothing declared') and conflicts ('No conflict declared') are stated (pp. 33–34).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are not met (2, no protocol; 4, the search; 7, no list of excluded studies; 13, risk of bias not carried into the conclusions) and a fifth (9) only partly, so confidence in the review as an accurate and comprehensive summary is critically low. The practical consequences: studies may be missing (PsycINFO yielded 10 records; English and Dutch only; 10 eligible full texts excluded by region); the synthesis gives no count of studies by direction and weights a 31%-response survey equally with a 92%-response one; and the conclusions about consequences for care outrun the few, mostly qualitative studies behind them while omitting one contrary observational study. The review may be cited for what the included studies reported, with their designs, and for the observation that few studies published by 2011 examined consequences of professionals' attitudes for care; it may not be cited for how common negative attitudes are, for a causal effect of attitudes on care or outcomes, or for training improving attitudes.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: PubMed 1170, PsycINFO 10 and Embase 395 records (1575 combined); 13 duplicates; 1562 titles screened and 1142 excluded; 420 abstracts screened and 365 excluded (31 because no abstract or full text was available, 34 concerning education, training or students); 55 full texts assessed and 27 excluded, 10 of them (37%) as Asian, African or South American studies; 28 included.

Searches covered articles published from January 2000 to November 2011 in English or Dutch; titles were screened by one reviewer with a random 10% screened by a second (94% agreement), and abstracts and full texts by two independent reviewers.

Quality was judged with 11 indicators from Buckley et al. (2009), acceptable if at least 7 were met; all 28 included papers met the criteria and were given equal weight; ratings by study are not reported.
key_findings.locator: 3.1 Search results, 1st paragraph (continued on p. 26); Table 3 (p. 26)

key_findings.finding: Of the 28 papers, 12 were from Australia, 7 the UK, 5 the USA, 1 Canada and 1 Ireland, with one eight-country European comparison and one USA–UK comparison. Twenty were quantitative (the Substance Abuse Attitude Survey in 5, the Alcohol and Alcohol Problems Perception Questionnaire in 4); five used interviews or focus groups, two implicit association tests and two observation; five also included patients.

Five of the included papers are marked as coming from shared samples: Brener et al. (2007, 2010a), 60 health care workers, and Ford et al. (2008, 2009) with Ford (2011), a survey of 1605 nurses in the Australian Capital Territory (the 2011 paper interprets one open-ended question, with N = 311).
key_findings.locator: Table 4, Brener and Ford rows and footnote

key_findings.finding: The review summarizes that health professionals generally had negative attitudes towards patients with substance use problems. Examples: regard was lowest for patients with drug and alcohol problems compared with depression or diabetes, among 866 professionals in 8 European countries, and lowest among physicians outside addiction services (Gilchrist et al., 2011); in six focus groups with 35 health and social care professionals, most preferred that addiction specialists provide the care (McLaughlin et al., 2006); nurses reported low motivation and satisfaction in caring for patients who use illicit drugs (Ford et al., 2008); in a vignette study professionals held more stigmatizing views of active substance use disorder than of other mental illness, and more positive views of recovery than of relapse (Rao et al., 2009).
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Attitudes of health professionals, 1st paragraph (p. 26, continued on p. 29); Table 4, Gilchrist et al. (2011) row (p. 28)
key_findings.note: Table 5's summary of Gilchrist et al. (2011) says both that regard did not differ by gender, age or professional group and that psychologists, social workers and addiction-service staff showed the highest regard and physicians outside addiction services the lowest (p. 31); the primary study is needed to settle which applies.

key_findings.finding: Positive or neutral findings: mental health professionals with generally positive and non-discriminatory attitudes, most rejecting moral stereotypes (Pinikahana et al., 2002), and primary care physicians with positive attitudes (Saitz et al., 2002), reported as a contrast. In Table 5, six of the study summaries describe attitudes as moderate (Giannetti et al., 2002), neutral (Happell & Taylor, 2001), appropriate (an unlabelled row on emergency departments), positive (Pinikahana et al., 2002; Saitz et al., 2002, who also report lower satisfaction) or below the criterion for negative stigma (Strauser et al., 2009).
key_findings.note: The count of six is the editors' reading of the Table 5 summaries; the review itself gives no count.

key_findings.finding: Five papers found more positive or different attitudes with more personal or work experience or contact (Brener et al., 2007; Ding et al., 2005; Giannetti et al., 2002; May et al., 2002; Russell et al., 2011). Anaesthesiologists were less positive than physicians who regularly treat these patients and more positive if they had a personal history of addiction (May et al., 2002); forensic psychiatric nurses were more negative than other mental health professionals (Foster & Onyeukwu, 2003).

Explanations offered: nurses described violence, manipulation and irresponsibility as barriers to care (Ford, 2011, an open-ended survey question); general practitioners perceived patients with drug problems as manipulative, aggressive, rude and poorly motivated (McGillion et al., 2000); higher perceived controllability of injecting drug use went with more negative attitudes (Brener et al., 2010a); professionals reported low knowledge (four studies); education improved nurses' therapeutic attitude only with at least moderate role support (Ford et al., 2008, 2009).
key_findings.locator: 3.4 Explanations for negative attitudes, 1st paragraph (p. 29) and 2nd to 4th paragraphs (p. 32); Table 5 (p. 30)

key_findings.finding: Consequences for care, quantitative: clients who reported more perceived discrimination by staff and dissatisfaction were less likely to complete treatment (cited in the text as Brener et al., 2010a; Table 5 gives this finding for Brener et al., 2010b, a mixed-methods study of 92 clients of residential rehabilitation services in Sydney); patients judged their professionals more favourably when the professionals had more positive attitudes (Brener et al., 2007); physicians' negative attitudes were not associated with patients' reported problems with care, dissatisfaction, unmet needs or perceived access (Ding et al., 2005: 2864 patients with HIV, 17.1% currently injecting, and 373 physicians, 75% response).
key_findings.locator: 3.5 Consequences of attitudes on healthcare delivery, 1st paragraph (p. 32, continued on p. 33); Table 4 (p. 27); Table 5 (p. 30)
key_findings.note: The Brener et al. (2007) statement is the review's text (p. 32); Table 5 summarizes that study differently (see reporting issues). The treatment-completion finding belongs to Brener et al. (2010b), not 2010a.

key_findings.finding: Consequences for care, qualitative: clinicians may unwittingly impose their beliefs on patients and impede collaboration (Curtis & Harrison, 2001: 57 participants, 26 of them consumers, in alcohol and other drug services); district nurses described shorter visits, visiting in pairs and a more task-oriented approach (Peckover & Chidlaw, 2007: 18 nurses, 82% response).

Segal & Dittrich (2001): 683 observed visits by patients to 9 psychiatric emergency services in California in 1985–1986; patients with substance use problems received better quality of care than other patients on all 4 study criteria, although clinicians' attitudes towards them were not always positive. The study is not mentioned in the text.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (p. 29) and Table 5 (p. 32), Segal and Dittrich rows

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: relevant studies may have been missed; records without an abstract or full text were excluded; only English and Dutch articles were included; the primary studies may suffer selection bias because only motivated professionals take part, and self-report and social desirability limit their quality.

The authors conclude that in most examined studies professionals expressed negative attitudes; that inadequate training, education and support may contribute; that more and longitudinal studies of consequences are needed; and that more education and training and organisational support may improve attitudes and care.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.5 attributes the finding that clients who perceived more staff discrimination were less likely to complete treatment to Brener et al. (2010a). In Tables 4 and 5 and the reference list, Brener et al. (2010a) is a study of 60 health care workers' attitudes, and the treatment-completion finding belongs to Brener et al. (2010b), titled as a study of perceived discriminatory treatment by staff as a predictor of treatment completion.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim using this finding must cite the primary study as Brener et al. (2010b, Drug and Alcohol Review 29, 491–497), a mixed-methods study of 92 clients of residential rehabilitation services in Sydney.

reporting_issues.issue: Segal & Dittrich (2001), the only included study that measured the quality of care actually delivered (observed psychiatric emergency visits), found better care for patients with substance use problems; it appears in Tables 4 and 5 but nowhere in the text, including the section on consequences.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's conclusion that negative attitudes contribute to suboptimal care leaves out the one contrary observational result it included; any claim about consequences for care must mention it (with its 1985–1986 data).

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 5 the row following Howard and Holmshaw (2010) has no study name and no instrument name; its content (a five-subscale attitude scale; appropriate attitudes and knowledge gaps in emergency departments) matches Kelleher and Cotter (2009), the emergency-department study in Table 4, which otherwise has no row in Table 5.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader would attribute the emergency-department findings to Howard and Holmshaw; the attribution to Kelleher and Cotter is the editors' inference and should be checked in the primary study before it is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that patients judged their professionals more favourably when the professionals had more positive attitudes (Brener et al., 2007), but Table 5's summary of that study links clients' favourable views to attending services with more people with hepatitis C, not to the professionals' attitudes.
reporting_issues.consequence: The link between professionals' attitudes and patients' views cannot be confirmed from the review; the primary study must be read before it is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Happell and Taylor (2001) is cited among studies that established positive effects of training and education on attitudes and perceived knowledge, but Table 5 reports that nurses who did and did not use a liaison service did not differ in attitudes (only perceived knowledge was higher); Ding et al. (2005), also cited, concerns knowledge rather than training in Table 5; and all four cited studies are cross-sectional.
reporting_issues.consequence: The evidence that training improves attitudes is thinner than the text implies and is associational; the review cannot support a causal claim about training.

reporting_issues.issue: PsycINFO contributed only 10 records, against 1170 from PubMed and 395 from Embase, without comment; the printed strategy retrieves only records that carry an attitude term together with a care-delivery or stigma term (sets #30 to #33).
reporting_issues.consequence: Attitude studies in the psychological literature, or indexed without care-delivery or stigma terms, may have been missed; the authors acknowledge only in general terms that relevant studies may not have been found.

reporting_issues.issue: Happell et al. (2002) and Pinikahana et al. (2002), by the same three authors in the same journal and year, both describe crisis assessment and treatment teams in metropolitan Melbourne and rural Victoria and both include 134 registered nurses, but they are not marked as sharing a sample.
reporting_issues.consequence: Possibly one more overlapping sample than the review flags; the 28 papers would then represent at most 24 independent samples (25 with the overlaps the review marks).

reporting_issues.issue: Subgroup counts in Table 4 do not add up to the stated totals: Gilchrist et al. (2011) give 866 professionals, broken down as 92, 80 and 81 by setting; Pinikahana et al. (2002) give 173, broken down as 134, 16, 12, 3 and 3 by profession; McLaughlin et al. (2006) give 35, with 9, 14, 3, 3 and 1 by profession plus two unnumbered roles. By the editors' arithmetic the breakdowns sum to 253, 168 and 30.
reporting_issues.consequence: Sample sizes from Table 4 should be checked in the primary studies before they are quoted; for Gilchrist et al. the breakdown may refer to something other than the whole sample.

reporting_issues.issue: The professional groups listed in 3.2 (seven mixed, eight nurses, seven addiction or mental health staff, four physicians, one physicians and nurses) add up to 27, not 28 papers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; one paper is unaccounted for in the description of populations.

reporting_issues.issue: Studies of a very specific setting or explicit subgroup were to be excluded (Study selection, p. 25), yet the included papers concern, among others, forensic psychiatric nurses, anaesthesiologists, physicians of patients with HIV who inject drugs, dual-diagnosis care and clients with hepatitis C; no list of exclusions shows how the rule was applied.
reporting_issues.consequence: The selection rule appears under-specified or unevenly applied, which adds to the uncertainty about which studies the review represents.
